name: Rosa Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at half five, make the kids' lunches, and I'm at the gate by seven. Right now we're building a block of council flats on Mill Lane, timber frame, four storeys, and I'm the newest carpenter on the crew. Mostly I'm fixing battens, cutting noggins, carrying sheets of ply up the scaffold, and asking Gary, the chargehand, a hundred questions a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on site? I understand it's fairly new for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I did fifteen years in a school canteen, until the council handed the kitchens to a private company and they cut half of us. The union rep got me onto a trades course for adults, and here I am at forty-three with sore knees and a nail gun. I like it, honestly. I like that at the end of the week there's a wall standing that wasn't there on Monday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being slow. The young lads cut a stair string in ten minutes and I'm still measuring twice, three times. And the cold in January, and my phone, which Gary says belongs in a museum. I don't do apps. Tomasz, my partner, he drives the number 14 bus, he does all that for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Every few months somebody on the news says a robot's coming for your job, and then nothing comes. I'd probably say it in the canteen hut, not online, because I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. I've just started over once, and I'm not good enough yet to start over again. If nothing changes, I get five more years to stop being the slow one on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Finish my second-year card, try to get on the next council job after Mill Lane, and keep putting a bit by each month into the savings, maybe eighty a month. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight off. I'd still have my usual worries, the mortgage and Lena's braces, but not the big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the canteen job going private. Does that history change how you'd see this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, because that wasn't a robot, that was a contract. So even with AI being hype, I know the danger is a company deciding we cost too much. The thing that saved me then was the union, not any gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena and Max at dinner if this is how it turned out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them they can stop asking me if robots are taking Mum's job. Max asks that, he's nine, he saw a video. I'd say Mum's going to keep building flats for people who need them, and they should eat their peas.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew in the hut that it was hype, like I always said. Every few months someone says a robot's coming for your job and then nothing happens.
S0.think: Privately it's relief, because I've only just started over once and I'm not good enough yet to do it again. It buys me time to stop being the slow one.
S0.do: Keeps working on the council flats, finishes her second-year card and tries to get onto the next council job. Keeps putting about 80 a month into savings.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with only the usual worries about the mortgage and her daughter's braces.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I get five more years to stop being the slow one on the crew.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa sees the threat to her work as coming from contracts and cost-cutting more than from machines, because that's what happened to her canteen job. She has no interest in technology and says so cheerfully. Her relief here is about time to catch up on skills, not about the economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before the firms bring it in, not after. That's what I'd say at the branch meeting. If jobs are changing, the workers should get the training and a say in how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared I'm the one who gets changed out. I'm forty-three, I'm the junior, and I'm the one who still asks how to set out a stud wall. If they bring in a machine that does the boring cutting, that boring cutting is most of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting, which I don't now, if I'm truthful. I'd ask the firm what training is coming and put my name down first. I wouldn't buy any gadgets or learn any app on my own though. I'd keep my head down and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, because it's slow and people still have work. But there's a knot there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your name down for training, but also that you wouldn't learn any app. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I mean training the firm gives, with a person teaching me, on site. I won't sit at home poking a phone. If Gary shows me how to run a cutting machine, I'll learn it. If it's a video, I'll forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, the labourer. He's fifty-eight and he carts everything around. A carrying robot would have him gone first. And me second, probably, because I'm not quick.

S1.say: I'd say at the union branch that workers need to be at the table before firms bring this in. The people whose jobs change should get the training and a say.
S1.think: I'm scared I'm the one who gets changed out, because the simple cutting a machine could take is most of what I do. Being 43 and the junior makes me feel exposed.
S1.do: Starts going to every union branch meeting and asks the firm to put her first on any training. Keeps working and refuses to learn apps on her own time.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot of worry but not panic, because the change is slow.
S1.quote: If they bring in a machine that does the boring cutting, that boring cutting is most of what I do.
S1.fieldNote: There's a gap between her public line about worker training and her private belief that she'll be first out. She'll learn from a person but not from a screen, which is a real limit in this picture. She worries more for an older labourer than for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the government's job now. Stop the firms throwing people out, pay people properly while it settles, and tax whoever owns the robots. I'd be at the march, with a sign, probably the one Tomasz painted for the canteen strike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished in trades. I've had two and a half years. I don't have a skill yet that a robot can't copy, and in two years I won't have one either. It's the canteen all over again, only this time there's nowhere to retrain to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the holiday we booked for August and put that money in savings. We've got about four months of bills put by, and I'd want six. I'd join the union campaign properly, give up Saturdays for it. If the job goes, I'd sign on and look for whatever's left that needs a person, maybe care work again, though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. It's that feeling when the manager called us in to the canteen office. I'd be lying awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what changes for you compared with a longer run-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. Two years isn't enough to get good at anything. With ten I could at least finish my card and maybe get into something like site inspections. With two, I'm the junior with half a trade when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first, if the money stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the mortgage, never the mortgage. It'd be the car first, we'd sell it and Tomasz's bus pass does the rest. Then the kids' swimming, which breaks my heart because Max just got his ten-metre badge.

S2.say: This is the government's job now: stop the firms throwing people out, pay people properly while it settles, and tax whoever owns the robots. I'd be at the march with a sign.
S2.think: I think I'm finished in trades, because two years isn't enough to build a skill a robot can't copy. It's losing the canteen job all over again, with nowhere to retrain to.
S2.do: Cancels the August holiday and moves that money into savings, aiming for six months of bills instead of four. Gives up Saturdays for the union campaign and would sell the car and sign on if the job goes.
S2.feel: Sick and sleepless, like being called into the manager's office again.
S2.quote: It's the canteen all over again, only this time there's nowhere to retrain to.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline lands on her worst point: half-trained and too late to switch again. Her response is collective and political, not personal reinvention, which fits both her outlook and her dislike of new technology. She knows exactly which things get sold first, which says a lot about how close the margin feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before but louder and earlier. Five years means there's time to fight for rules, like a law that a building site has to keep a share of human workers, or retraining money that's real. I'd be telling everyone at the branch: this is the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I'd be forty-eight when it lands. Old enough that nobody wants to train me up again, young enough that I've got fifteen years of mortgage left. I think it means I'd have just got good at carpentry and then lose it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to finish my card in the next eighteen months so at least I'm a qualified carpenter, not a trainee, when the cuts start. We'd overpay the mortgage a bit, maybe a hundred a month, and keep building savings. And I'd stand for union rep on site, which I'd never have done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years is better than two, but it's like watching a lorry coming down the road slowly. You still can't get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for union rep. What would you actually push for on Mill Lane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the firm tells us a year ahead before any robot comes on site, and that nobody gets let go without the firm paying for a new course. And that the older ones like Dennis get to finish out properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz about the mortgage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's get it down while we both still earn. His bus could go driverless too, he jokes about it. So it's both of us in this, and I'd rather owe less when it comes.

S3.say: Five years is the window to fight for rules, like keeping a share of human workers on sites and real retraining money. I'd be telling everyone at the branch to act now.
S3.think: I'd be 48 when it lands, too old for anyone to train me again but with 15 years of mortgage left. I'd finally get good at carpentry just in time to lose it.
S3.do: Aims to finish her carpentry card within 18 months and overpays the mortgage by about 100 a month. Stands for union rep on site and pushes for a year's notice before robots arrive.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a lorry come down the road slowly.
S3.quote: Old enough that nobody wants to train me up again, young enough that I've got fifteen years of mortgage left.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts her from shock to organising: she'd step up as a rep, something she says she'd never do now. Her personal plan is to get qualified quickly, not to change field. Both she and her partner have jobs exposed to automation, which raises the stakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse. Plan the training, plan the pensions, plan who gets what from the machines. If governments don't use a decade, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get maybe eight good years in a trade I chose. I'd be fifty-three when it all arrives. I think I'd survive it, but I don't see myself learning to run robots. Someone younger will do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my card, keep working, and keep the union campaign going. I'd put the extra into the kids, so Lena could do something with people, nursing maybe, something a machine won't be trusted with. For myself I'd probably wait and see what the union wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. It's far enough away that I can sleep. But it's the same end, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you want to retrain into something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. I retrained once at forty. I'm not doing it again at fifty for a job that might also go. I'd rather fight for a decent landing than chase the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about her own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick something where people need to look you in the eye. Nursing, teaching little ones. And join the union on your first day, like your mum should have done earlier.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to plan the training, the pensions and who gets what from the machines, so there's no excuse. If governments waste a decade, that's on them.
S4.think: I get maybe eight good years in a trade I chose, and I'd be 53 when it all arrives. I'd survive it, but I don't see myself learning to run robots.
S4.do: Finishes her carpentry card, keeps working and keeps up the union campaign. Steers her daughter towards nursing or other people-facing work and waits to see what the union wins.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a bit sad, though it's far enough away to sleep at night.
S4.quote: I retrained once at forty. I'm not doing it again at fifty for a job that might also go.
S4.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't make Rosa want to retrain; it makes her want to dig in and organise. She puts her hopes into her daughter's choices instead of her own reinvention. Her refusal is clear-eyed rather than in denial.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. I'd be caught half-trained with no time to do anything. What would help is money that keeps the mortgage paid while people sort themselves out, and the firms not being allowed to just drop us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who builds the houses. We're on council flats because people can't afford rent. If robots build them cheaper, fine, but who's living in them if nobody's got a wage? That's the bit nobody on TV answers.

headlineQuote: If robots build them cheaper, fine, but who's living in them if nobody's got a wage?
portrait: Rosa Ziegler is 43 and two and a half years into carpentry, after losing a school canteen job when the kitchens were outsourced. She works on a council flats build, still slow and still learning, and she doesn't use apps or AI. Through the five pictures she stays rooted in the union and in politics rather than personal reinvention: relieved by the plateau, alarmed by AGI in two years, and organising harder as the warning time grows. With ten years she'd still refuse to retrain a second time and would steer her daughter towards people-facing work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be caught half-trained with no time to do anything.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that keeps the mortgage paid while people adjust, and rules that stop firms simply dropping workers.
